section.heading: 5.1 Eigenvectors and Eigenvalues
section.paragraph: Although a transformation $$\textbf{x}\mapsto A\textbf{x}$$ may move vectors in a variety of directions, it often happens that there are special vectors on which the action of $$A$$ is quite simple.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Let $$A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 3 & {- 2} \\ 1 & 0 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\textbf{u} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 1} \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , and $$\textbf{v} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 2 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . The images of $$\textbf{u}$$ and v under multiplication by $$A$$ are shown in Figure 1. In fact, $$A\textbf{v}$$ is just $$2\textbf{v}$$ . So $$A$$ only “stretches” or dilates v.

image.alt: A graph shows four vectors and two dotted arrows pointing between two pairs of vectors.

section.paragraph: This section studies equations such as
$$A \textbf{x} = 2 \textbf{x} \text{or} A \textbf{x} = - 4 \textbf{x}$$
where special vectors are transformed by $$A$$ into scalar multiples of themselves.

note.paragraph: An eigenvector of an $$n \times n$$ matrix $$A$$ is a nonzero vector $$\textbf{x}$$ such that $$A\textbf{x} = \text{λ} \textbf{x}$$ for some scalar $$\text{λ}$$ . A scalar $$\text{λ}$$ is called an eigenvalue of $$A$$ if there is a nontrivial solution $$\textbf{x}$$ of $$A\textbf{x} = \text{λ} \textbf{x};$$ such an $$\textbf{x}$$ is called an eigenvector corresponding to $$\text{λ}$$ .1

section.paragraph: It is easy to determine if a given vector is an eigenvector of a matrix. See Example 2. It is also easy to decide if a specified scalar is an eigenvalue. See Example 3.

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Let $$A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 1 & 6 \\ 5 & 2 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\textbf{u} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 6 \\ {- 5} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , and $$\textbf{v} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 3 \\ {- 2} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Are $$\textbf{u}$$ and v eigenvectors of $$A$$ ?
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: $$A \textbf{u} & = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}1 & 6 \\ 5 & 2\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}6 \\ - 5\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}- 24 \\ 20\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} = - 4 \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}6 \\ - 5\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} = - 4 \textbf{u} A \textbf{v} & = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}1 & 6 \\ 5 & 2\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}3 \\ - 2\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}- 9 \\ 11\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \neq \lambda \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}3 \\ - 2\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix}$$
Thus $$\textbf{u}$$ is an eigenvector corresponding to an eigenvalue $$( - 4)$$ , but v is not an eigenvector of $$A$$ , because $$A\textbf{v}$$ is not a multiple of $$v$$ .

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Show that $$7$$ is an eigenvalue of matrix $$A$$ in Example 2, and find the corresponding eigenvectors.
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The scalar $$7$$ is an eigenvalue of $$A$$ if and only if the equation
$$A \textbf{x} = 7 \textbf{x}$$
has a nontrivial solution. But (1) is equivalent to $$A\textbf{x} - 7\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ , or
$$\left(\right. A - 7 I \left.\right) \textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$
To solve this homogeneous equation, form the matrix
$$A - 7 I = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 6 \\ 5 & 2 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 7 & 0 \\ 0 & 7 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} - 6 & 6 \\ 5 & - 5 \end{bmatrix}$$
The columns of $$A - 7I$$ are obviously linearly dependent, so (2) has nontrivial solutions. Thus $$7$$ is an eigenvalue of $$A$$ . To find the corresponding eigenvectors, use row operations:
$$\begin{bmatrix} - 6 & 6 & 0 \\ 5 & - 5 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$

The general solution has the form $$x_{2}\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Each vector of this form with $$x_{2} \neq 0$$ is an eigenvector corresponding to $$\text{λ} = 7$$ .

section.paragraph: Warning: Although row reduction was used in Example 3 to find eigenvectors, it cannot be used to find eigenvalues. An echelon form of a matrix $$A$$ usually does not display the eigenvalues of $$A$$ .

The equivalence of equations (1) and (2) obviously holds for any $$\text{λ}$$ in place of $$\text{λ} = 7$$ . Thus $$\text{λ}$$ is an eigenvalue of an $$n \times n$$ matrix $$A$$ if and only if the equation
$$\left(\right. A - \lambda I \left.\right) \textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$

has a nontrivial solution. The set of all solutions of (3) is just the null space of the matrix $$A - \text{λ} I$$ . So this set is a subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ and is called the eigenspace of $$A$$ corresponding to $$\text{λ}$$ . The eigenspace consists of the zero vector and all the eigenvectors corresponding to $$\text{λ}$$ .

Example 3 shows that for matrix $$A$$ in Example 2, the eigenspace corresponding to $$\text{λ} = 7$$ consists of all multiples of $$(1,1)$$ , which is the line through $$(1,1)$$ and the origin. From Example 2, you can check that the eigenspace corresponding to $$\text{λ} = - 4$$ is the line through $$(6, - 5)$$ . These eigenspaces are shown in Figure 2, along with eigenvectors $$(1,1)$$ and $$(3/2, - 5/4)$$ and the geometric action of the transformation $$\textbf{x}\mapsto A\textbf{x}$$ on each eigenspace.

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Let $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & {- 1} & 6 \\ 2 & 1 & 6 \\ 2 & {- 1} & 8 \end{bmatrix}$$ . An eigenvalue of $$A$$ is $$2$$ . Find a basis for the corresponding eigenspace.
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Form

$$A - 2 I = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & - 1 & 6 \\ 2 & 1 & 6 \\ 2 & - 1 & 8 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & - 1 & 6 \\ 2 & - 1 & 6 \\ 2 & - 1 & 6 \end{bmatrix}$$
and row reduce the augmented matrix for $$(A - 2I)\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ :
At this point, it is clear that $$2$$ is indeed an eigenvalue of $$A$$ because the equation $$(A - 2I)\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ has free variables. The general solution is

$$\begin{bmatrix} x_{1} \\ x_{2} \\ x_{3} \end{bmatrix} = x_{2 } \begin{bmatrix} 1 / 2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + x_{3} \begin{bmatrix} - 3 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} , x_{2} \text{and} x_{3} \text{free}$$
The eigenspace, shown in Figure 3, is a two-dimensional subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ . A basis is
$$\begin{Bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} , \begin{bmatrix} - 3 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \end{Bmatrix}$$

note.title: Reasonable Answers
note.heading: Reasonable Answers
note.paragraph: Remember that once you find a potential eigenvector $$\textbf{v}$$ , you can easily check your answer: just find $$A\textbf{v}$$ and see if it is a multiple of $$\textbf{v}$$ . For example, to check whether $$\textbf{v} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ is an eigenvector of $$A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 1 & 2 \\ {- 1} & {- 2} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , notice $$A\textbf{v} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 3 \\ {- 3} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , which is not a multiple of $$\textbf{v} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , establishing that $$\textbf{v}$$ is not an eigenvector. It turns out we had a sign error. The vector $$\textbf{u} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ {- 1} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ is a correct eigenvector for $$A$$ since $$A\textbf{u} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 1} \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack = - 1\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ {- 1} \end{array} \right\rbrack = - 1\textbf{u}$$ .

note.title: Numerical Notes﻿
note.heading: Numerical Notes﻿
note.paragraph: Example 4 shows a good method for manual computation of eigenvectors in simple cases when an eigenvalue is known. Using a matrix program and row reduction to find an eigenspace (for a specified eigenvalue) usually works, too, but this is not entirely reliable. Roundoff error can lead occasionally to a reduced echelon form with the wrong number of pivots. The best computer programs compute approximations for eigenvalues and eigenvectors simultaneously, to any desired degree of accuracy, for matrices that are not too large. The size of matrices that can be analyzed increases each year as computing power and software improve.

section.paragraph: The following theorem describes one of the few special cases in which eigenvalues can be found precisely. Calculation of eigenvalues will also be discussed in Section 5.2.

note.title: Theorem ﻿1﻿
note.heading: Theorem ﻿1﻿
note.paragraph: The eigenvalues of a triangular matrix are the entries on its main diagonal.

section.heading: Proof
section.paragraph: For simplicity, consider the $$3 \times 3$$ case. If $$A$$ is upper triangular, then $$A - \text{λ} I$$ has the form

$$A - \lambda I & = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}a_{11} & a_{12} & a_{13} \\ 0 & a_{22} & a_{23} \\ 0 & 0 & a_{33}\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}\lambda & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \lambda\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} & = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}a_{11} - \lambda & a_{12} & a_{13} \\ 0 & a_{22} - \lambda & a_{23} \\ 0 & 0 & a_{33} - \lambda\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix}$$

The scalar $$\text{λ}$$ is an eigenvalue of $$A$$ if and only if the equation $$(A - \text{λ} I)\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ has a nontrivial solution, that is, if and only if the equation has a free variable. Because of the zero entries in $$A - \text{λ} I$$ , it is easy to see that $$(A - \text{λ} I)\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ has a free variable if and only if at least one of the entries on the diagonal of $$A - \text{λ} I$$ is zero. This happens if and only if $$\text{λ}$$ equals one of the entries $$a_{11}$$ , $$a_{22}$$ , $$a_{33}$$ in $$A$$ . For the case in which $$A$$ is lower triangular, see Exercise 36.

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Let $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & { 6} & {- 8} \\ 0 & { 0} & { 6} \\ 0 & { 0} & { 2} \end{bmatrix}$$ and $$B = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rrr} 4 & 0 & 0 \\ {- 2} & 1 & 0 \\ 5 & 3 & 4 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . The eigenvalues of $$A$$ are $$3$$ , $$0$$ , and $$2$$ . The eigenvalues of $$B$$ are $$4$$ and $$1$$ .

section.paragraph: What does it mean for a matrix $$A$$ to have an eigenvalue of $$0$$ , such as in Example 5? This happens if and only if the equation
$$A \textbf{x} = 0 \textbf{x}$$

has a nontrivial solution. But (4) is equivalent to $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ , which has a nontrivial solution if and only if $$A$$ is not invertible. Thus $$0$$ is an eigenvalue of $$A$$ if and only if $$A$$ is not invertible. This fact will be added to the Invertible Matrix Theorem in Section 5.2.

The following important theorem will be needed later. Its proof illustrates a typical calculation with eigenvectors. One way to prove the statement “If $$P$$ then $$Q$$ ” is to show that $$P$$ and the negation of $$Q$$ leads to a contradiction. This strategy is used in the proof of the theorem.

note.title: Theorem ﻿2﻿
note.heading: Theorem ﻿2﻿
note.paragraph: If $$\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{r}$$ are eigenvectors that correspond to distinct eigenvalues $$\text{λ} _{1},\ldots, \text{λ} _{r}$$ of an $$n \times n$$ matrix $$A$$ , then the set $$\{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{r}\}$$ is linearly independent.

section.heading: Proof
section.paragraph: Suppose $$\{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{r}\}$$ is linearly dependent. Since $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ is nonzero, Theorem 7 in Section 1.7 says that one of the vectors in the set is a linear combination of the preceding vectors. Let $$p$$ be the least index such that $$\textbf{v}_{p + 1}$$ is a linear combination of the preceding (linearly independent) vectors. Then there exist scalars $$c_{1},\ldots,c_{p}$$ such that
$$c_{1} \textbf{v}_{1} + \hdots + c_{p} \textbf{v}_{p} = \textbf{v}_{p + 1}$$
Multiplying both sides of (5) by $$A$$ and using the fact that $$A\textbf{v}_{k} = \text{λ} _{k}\textbf{v}_{k}$$ for each $$k$$ , we obtain
$$c_{1} A v_{1} + \hdots + c_{p} A v_{p} & = & A v_{p + 1} c_{1} \lambda_{1} v_{1} + \hdots + c_{p} \lambda_{p} v_{p} & = & \lambda_{p + 1} v_{p + 1}$$
Multiplying both sides of (5) by $$\text{λ} _{p + 1}$$ and subtracting the result from (6), we have
$$c_{1} \left(\right. \lambda_{1} - \lambda_{p + 1} \left.\right) \textbf{v}_{1} + \hdots + c_{p} \left(\right. \lambda_{p} - \lambda_{p + 1} \left.\right) \textbf{v}_{p} = \textbf{0}$$

Since $$\{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}\}$$ is linearly independent, the weights in (7) are all zero. But none of the factors $$\text{λ} _{i} - \text{λ} _{p + 1}$$ are zero, because the eigenvalues are distinct. Hence $$c_{i} = 0$$ for $$i = 1,\ldots,p$$ . But then (5) says that $$\textbf{v}_{p + 1} = \textbf{0}$$ , which is impossible. Hence $$\{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{r}\}$$ cannot be linearly dependent and therefore must be linearly independent.
section.heading: Eigenvectors and Difference Equations
section.paragraph: This section concludes by showing how to construct solutions of the first-order difference equation discussed in the chapter introductory example:
$$\textbf{x}_{k + 1} = A \textbf{x}_{k} \left(\right. k = 0 , 1 , 2 , \ldots \left.\right)$$

If $$A$$ is an $$n \times n$$ matrix, then (8) is a recursive description of a sequence $$\{\textbf{x}_{k}\}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ . A solution of (8) is an explicit description of $$\{\textbf{x}_{k}\}$$ whose formula for each $$\textbf{x}_{k}$$ does not depend directly on $$A$$ or on the preceding terms in the sequence other than the initial term $$\textbf{x}_{0}$$ .
The simplest way to build a solution of (8) is to take an eigenvector $$\textbf{x}_{0}$$ and its corresponding eigenvalue $$\text{λ}$$ and let
$$\textbf{x}_{k} = \lambda^{k} \textbf{x}_{0} \left(\right. k = 1 , 2 , \ldots \left.\right)$$
This sequence is a solution because

$$A \textbf{x}_{k} = A \left(\right. \lambda^{k} \textbf{x}_{0} \left.\right) = \lambda^{k} \left(\right. A \textbf{x}_{0} \left.\right) = \lambda^{k} \left(\right. \lambda \textbf{x}_{0} \left.\right) = \lambda^{k + 1} \textbf{x}_{0} = \textbf{x}_{k + 1}$$
Linear combinations of solutions in the form of equation (9) are solutions, too! See Exercise 41.

list.item: If $$\textbf{x}$$ is an eigenvector of $$A$$ corresponding to $$\text{λ}$$ , what is $$A^{3}\textbf{x}$$ ?

Suppose that $$\textbf{b}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{b}_{2}$$ are eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues $$\text{λ} _{1}$$ and $$\text{λ} _{2}$$ , respectively, and suppose that $$\textbf{b}_{3}$$ and $$\textbf{b}_{4}$$ are linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to a third distinct eigenvalue $$\text{λ} _{3}$$ . Does it necessarily follow that $$\{\textbf{b}_{1},\textbf{b}_{2},\textbf{b}_{3},\textbf{b}_{4}\}$$ is a linearly independent set? [Hint: Consider the equation $$c_{1}\textbf{b}_{1} + c_{2}\textbf{b}_{2} + (c_{3}\textbf{b}_{3} + c_{4}\textbf{b}_{4}) = \textbf{0}$$ .]
If $$A$$ is an $$n \times n$$ matrix and $$\text{λ}$$ is an eigenvalue of $$A$$ , show that $$2 \text{λ}$$ is an eigenvalue of $$2A$$ .

section.paragraph: 1 Note that an eigenvector must be nonzero, by definition, but an eigenvalue may be zero. The case in which the number $$0$$ is an eigenvalue is discussed after Example 5.
